lesson.title: Gilded, Not Golden: Politics in an Age of Excess
lesson.summary: Mark Twain's sarcastic label for the post Civil War era captured a politics that looked impressive on the surface, packed rallies and razor close elections, but was often hollow and corrupt underneath, shaped by patronage and the interests of big business.
lesson.body:
The term "Gilded Age" comes from an 1873 satirical novel by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, "The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today." To be gilded means to be coated in a thin layer of gold over something cheaper underneath, and the title was a deliberate jab at an era of flashy new wealth built on shaky, often corrupt foundations. Historians generally use the term for the period running from the end of Reconstruction through the 1890s.

The industrialists and financiers covered as the era's Robber Barons, the men who built vast fortunes in railroads, steel, and oil, wielded enormous political influence during this period. They funded campaigns, lobbied for favorable tariffs and land grants, and in some documented cases bought legislators outright. Politics and business were tightly intertwined, and national elections were extraordinarily close: the disputed 1876 election between Rutherford Hayes and Samuel Tilden was resolved only through the backroom Compromise of 1877, and in 1888 Grover Cleveland actually won more popular votes than Benjamin Harrison yet still lost the presidency in the electoral college.

The same dynamic played out at the city level through Political Machines, urban organizations like New York's Tammany Hall, led for years by "Boss" William Tweed until his 1873 conviction, which traded government jobs, favors, and services for votes and loyalty, often skimming public funds through kickbacks and inflated contracts. Nationally, this took the form of the spoils system, in which the winning party after each election handed out federal jobs to loyal supporters rather than to qualified workers, a practice that produced waste, incompetence, and, as later chapters cover, an eventual and serious reform movement.

The two major parties drew on different bases: Republicans generally represented business interests, high protective tariffs, and Union Civil War veterans, a large and politically powerful pension constituency, and dominated much of the North, while Democrats controlled the "Solid South" after the end of Reconstruction and drew support from immigrant heavy urban political machines, generally favoring lower tariffs. Even within the Republican Party, factions calling themselves Stalwarts, who defended the spoils system outright, and Half Breeds, who leaned toward reform, fought bitterly over control of federal patronage, a fight that would turn deadly with the assassination of President James Garfield in 1881.
